tracks.title: Piazza Pitti — Before you go in
tracks.where: On Piazza Pitti, facing the palace. The ticket office is on the right-hand side of the façade; the way in is the central portal into the Ammannati Courtyard, where the main staircase and the lifts are on the right-hand side.
tracks.what: The long rusticated stone front of Palazzo Pitti, begun in the fifteenth century for the banker Luca Pitti, later home to the Medici, the Habsburg-Lorraine grand dukes and the kings of Italy.
tracks.listen: How a banker's house became the seat of three dynasties, and how the museums inside are laid out.

tracks.title: The Palatine Gallery — Antechamber and Gallery of the Statues
tracks.where: In the first rooms of the Palatine Gallery on the first floor: the antechamber, then the long Gallery of the Statues that leads to the Castagnoli Room.
tracks.what: An antechamber and a long gallery lined with classical marble statues; beyond them, rooms whose walls are covered with paintings in heavy gilded frames.
tracks.listen: What kind of gallery the Palatine is, why it's hung so densely, and which way the route runs.

tracks.title: The Castagnoli Room
tracks.where: In the Castagnoli Room, at the end of the Gallery of the Statues: the room with the large round inlaid-stone table at its centre.
tracks.what: Early nineteenth-century painted decoration by Giuseppe Castagnoli on the walls; at the centre, the Table of the Muses, in this room since 1855.
tracks.listen: Why this room sits between two worlds of the palace, and why the table in the middle is the thing to see.

tracks.title: The Table of the Muses
tracks.where: Beside the round table in the centre of the Castagnoli Room. Walk around it slowly, without touching or leaning on it.
tracks.what: A large round table of Florentine stone inlay, begun in the 1830s by Aristodemo Costoli and Giovan Battista Giorgi, on a bronze base modelled by Giovanni Dupré in the 1850s and cast by Clemente Papi; in this room since 1855.
tracks.listen: How a picture is made out of stone, and how long one table took.

tracks.title: Filippo Lippi — The Bartolini Tondo
tracks.where: In the Sala di Prometeo, in front of Filippo Lippi's large round panel. Stand close enough to see the small scenes in the background.
tracks.what: Filippo Lippi, Madonna and Child with Scenes from the Life of Saint Anne, known as the Bartolini Tondo, about 1452–53, tempera on wood, 135 cm across.
tracks.listen: How a friar packed three moments of one family's story into a single circle.

tracks.title: Raphael — Madonna dell'Impannata
tracks.where: In the Sala di Ulisse, in front of Raphael's Madonna dell'Impannata. Stand back far enough to see the whole group and the window behind it.
tracks.what: Raphael and workshop, Madonna dell'Impannata, 1511–12, oil on panel, 160 × 126 cm: the Virgin and Child with Saint Elizabeth, a younger female saint, and the infant John the Baptist.
tracks.listen: A banker's wedding picture, a duke's confiscation, and a restoration that changed what we think Raphael painted himself.

tracks.title: Cristofano Allori — Judith with the Head of Holofernes
tracks.where: In the Sala dell'Educazione di Giove, in front of Allori's Judith. Start close, then take a step back.
tracks.what: Cristofano Allori, Judith with the Head of Holofernes, 1610–12, oil on canvas, 139 × 116 cm.
tracks.listen: A painter who gave the severed head his own face, and the woman he painted as his executioner.

tracks.title: Caravaggio — Sleeping Cupid
tracks.where: Usually hung in the Sala dell'Educazione di Giove, near Allori's Judith; if it is not on the wall, ask the room staff where it is currently shown. Stand close.
tracks.what: Caravaggio, Sleeping Cupid, 1608, oil on canvas, about 72 × 105 cm: a small winged child asleep in the dark, his bow and arrows set aside.
tracks.listen: A painting that reached Florence while its painter was on the run, and why this Cupid is not as sweet as he looks.

tracks.title: Sala della Stufa — The Grand Duke's Hot Room
tracks.where: In the Sala della Stufa, the small room after the Sala dell'Educazione di Giove, just before the door to the atrium of the Moor's Staircase and the Sala dell'Iliade. Stand in the middle so you can turn to each wall.
tracks.what: Pietro da Cortona's wall frescoes of the Four Ages of Man, Golden and Silver Ages 1637, Bronze and Iron Ages 1641; the ceiling is by Cinganelli, Rosselli and Vannini.
tracks.listen: The Grand Duke's private heated bath, the fresco cycle that brought a new style to Florence, and where to go next.

tracks.title: Sala dell'Iliade — The Room of the Iliad
tracks.where: In the Sala dell'Iliade, entered from the Sala della Stufa through the atrium of the Moor's Staircase. Stand near the marble group in the centre and look up at the ceiling.
tracks.what: A large room under Luigi Sabatelli's ceiling of scenes from Homer's Iliad, begun in 1819, its walls hung with paintings and Lorenzo Bartolini's marble Charity at the centre.
tracks.listen: How a private corner of the Medici apartments became a room of Homer's war, and the three works here that have their own tracks.

tracks.title: Andrea del Sarto — The Passerini Assumption
tracks.where: In the Sala dell'Iliade, in front of the tall altarpiece of the Virgin rising above the apostles around her tomb. Step back far enough to take in both halves.
tracks.what: Andrea del Sarto, Assumption of the Virgin, known as the Assunta Passerini, oil on panel, 1526–28, almost four metres tall.
tracks.listen: Why two saints who were never at the tomb kneel in the best seats, and the woman in Cortona who paid for the picture.

tracks.title: Lorenzo Bartolini — Charity
tracks.where: In the Sala dell'Iliade, beside the white marble group at the centre of the room. Walk round it until you find the scroll in a child's hands.
tracks.what: Lorenzo Bartolini, Charity, marble, designed in the early 1820s and finished about 1835: a mother with two children, one of them holding a scroll with a Latin inscription.
tracks.listen: Why this gentle marble mother is really a teacher, and the sentence carved on the child's scroll.

tracks.title: Artemisia Gentileschi — Judith and her Maidservant
tracks.where: In front of Artemisia Gentileschi's Judith and her Maidservant, two women in a dark tent with a sword and a basket. It hangs here in the Sala dell'Iliade.
tracks.what: Artemisia Gentileschi, Judith and her Maidservant, oil on canvas, painted in her Florentine years.
tracks.listen: Why Artemisia paints the minute after the killing rather than the killing itself, and what the two women's partnership says.

tracks.title: Sala di Saturno — The Room of Raphael
tracks.where: In the Sala di Saturno, the first of the five Planet Rooms on the normal route. Stand in the middle of the room, where you can see the ceiling and the Raphaels on the walls.
tracks.what: A grand reception room under Ciro Ferri's ceiling of an aged prince led up to Saturn, god of Time, to be crowned by Fame; on the walls, the heart of the Pitti's Raphael collection.
tracks.listen: What this room meant in the Medici court, what the ceiling says, and how the room lets you follow Raphael from young Florentine painter to papal star.

tracks.title: Raphael — Madonna della Seggiola
tracks.where: In the Sala di Saturno, in front of the round painting of the Virgin hugging her child, with the young Saint John at the right edge.
tracks.what: Raphael, Madonna and Child with the Young Saint John, known as the Madonna della Seggiola, oil on panel, around 1512, a tondo about 71 centimetres across.
tracks.listen: The legend of the woman in the Roman doorway, the papal chair that undercuts it, and how three figures were fitted into a circle.

tracks.title: Raphael — La Gravida
tracks.where: In the Sala di Saturno, in front of Raphael's half-length portrait of a young woman against a black background, one hand on her belly and the other holding a glove. This painting used to hang in the Iliad Room; the museum now lists it here.
tracks.what: Raphael, Portrait of a Woman, known as La Gravida, oil on panel, around 1507, about 67 by 53 centimetres.
tracks.listen: Who she might have been, where her nickname came from, and why we can't be sure it's true.

tracks.title: Raphael — Pope Leo X with Two Cardinals
tracks.where: In the Sala di Saturno, in front of the large, dark portrait of a seated pope at a table, with a cardinal standing on either side behind him. Get close enough to see the golden knob on the back of his chair.
tracks.what: Raphael, Portrait of Pope Leo X with Cardinals Giulio de' Medici and Luigi de' Rossi, oil on panel, 1518.
tracks.listen: Who the pope and his two cousins were, the book and the magnifying glass on his table, and the tiny reflection that made the painting famous.

tracks.title: Raphael — Madonna del Granduca
tracks.where: In the Sala di Saturno, in front of the small, dark painting of the Virgin standing with the Christ Child in her arms against a black background.
tracks.what: Raphael, Madonna del Granduca, oil on panel, around 1506–07, about 84 by 56 centimetres.
tracks.listen: Why this Madonna stands in darkness Raphael never painted, and the grand duke who gave her a name and wouldn't let her go.

tracks.title: Raphael — Madonna del Baldacchino
tracks.where: In the Sala di Saturno, in front of the largest Raphael in the room: the Virgin enthroned beneath a great canopy, with four saints and two small angels at her feet. Step back first to take in the whole painting.
tracks.what: Raphael, Madonna del Baldacchino, oil on canvas, begun around 1507 and left unfinished; enlarged at the top for Grand Prince Ferdinando de' Medici after 1697.
tracks.listen: The altarpiece Raphael walked away from when Rome called, and the long road it took to this room.

tracks.title: Raphael — Portraits of Agnolo and Maddalena Doni
tracks.where: In the Sala di Saturno, in front of the pair of matching half-length portraits of a husband and wife. Look for the young woman's jewelled pendant.
tracks.what: Raphael, Portraits of Agnolo and Maddalena Doni, oil on basswood panel, around 1504–07, each about 63 by 45 centimetres; with the Flood painted on the back of his and its aftermath, Deucalion and Pyrrha, on the back of hers. The museum credits the painted backs to the Master of Serumido.
tracks.listen: A rich merchant, his teenage noble bride, the Leonardo portrait Raphael seems to have studied, and the flood painted on the back.

tracks.title: Sala di Giove — The Throne Room
tracks.where: In the Sala di Giove, the Room of Jupiter, between the Saturn and Mars rooms. Stand near the middle and look up at the vault.
tracks.what: Pietro da Cortona's ceiling of Jupiter crowning a young Medici prince, painted in the early 1640s; on the walls, Raphael's La Velata and Andrea del Sarto's young Saint John the Baptist.
tracks.listen: Why this was the Medici throne room, and the compliment to Galileo's moons hidden in the ceiling.

tracks.title: Raphael — La Velata (The Veiled Lady)
tracks.where: In the Sala di Giove, in front of Raphael's portrait of a woman in white silk with a veil over her hair.
tracks.what: Raphael, Portrait of a Woman, known as La Velata, oil on canvas, around 1512–15.
tracks.listen: Whether she was Raphael's beloved Fornarina or a married noblewoman, and how he paints white on white.

tracks.title: Andrea del Sarto — Young Saint John the Baptist
tracks.where: In the Sala di Giove, in front of Andrea del Sarto's young Saint John the Baptist: a youth half-wrapped in bright red drapery against a dark background, holding a scroll.
tracks.what: Andrea del Sarto, Saint John the Baptist, oil on panel, around 1523, 94 by 68 centimetres.
tracks.listen: A banker's commission, a saint painted from a living model who reminds many people of a statue, and Vasari's double-edged praise.

tracks.title: Sala di Marte — The Room of Mars
tracks.where: In the Sala di Marte, the third of the five Planet Rooms on today's route, entered from the Sala di Giove. Stand near the middle and look up at the ceiling first.
tracks.what: A grand reception room under Pietro da Cortona's ceiling fresco of Mars, painted in the mid-1640s. The room is traditionally home to Rubens's Consequences of War.
tracks.listen: Why the Medici prince's education reads backwards on today's route, what Cortona does with war, and the one work to find here.

tracks.title: Rubens — The Consequences of War
tracks.where: In the Sala di Marte, in front of the large Rubens allegory: an armoured Mars striding forward, a woman clinging to him, figures fallen underfoot. The painting normally hangs in the Sala di Marte; if it isn't here, ask an attendant.
tracks.what: Peter Paul Rubens, The Consequences of War, painted 1637–38 for the Medici court painter Justus Sustermans; bought by Grand Prince Ferdinando de' Medici in 1691.
tracks.listen: A painting that came with the painter's own explanation, read figure by figure, and how it reached the Medici.

tracks.title: Sala di Apollo — The Room of Apollo
tracks.where: In the Sala di Apollo, the fourth Planet Room on today's route, entered from the Sala di Marte. The Sala di Venere, the last room, is beyond it.
tracks.what: A grand reception room whose ceiling of Apollo, god of poetry, music and light, was begun by Pietro da Cortona and completed by his pupil Ciro Ferri. Titian's Penitent Magdalene hangs here.
tracks.listen: The schoolroom stage of the prince's education, a ceiling finished by two hands about a dozen years apart, and the painting to find first.

tracks.title: Titian — The Penitent Magdalene
tracks.where: In the Sala di Apollo, in front of Titian's half-length Magdalene: a woman covered by her long copper-gold hair, looking upward.
tracks.what: Titian, The Penitent Magdalene, 1531–35, oil on canvas, probably painted for Francesco Maria della Rovere, Duke of Urbino; in Florence since Vittoria della Rovere's inheritance of 1631.
tracks.listen: Who the Magdalene was in legend, the painting's double life as devotion and display, and how it came from Urbino to Florence.

tracks.title: Sala di Venere — The Room of Venus
tracks.where: In the Sala di Venere, the last room of today's Palatine route and the first room of the old Medici sequence. Canova's marble Venus stands in the centre.
tracks.what: A grand reception room with a ceiling fresco by Pietro da Cortona on the theme of Venus, Canova's Venus Italica at its centre, and three Titians on the walls: The Concert, Pietro Aretino and La Bella.
tracks.listen: Why the last room of your visit was the first room of the Medici's, and the four works waiting here.

tracks.title: Canova — Venus Italica
tracks.where: In the centre of the Sala di Venere, beside Canova's marble Venus. Walk all the way round her as you listen.
tracks.what: Antonio Canova, Venus Italica, completed 1812, marble, about 172 cm tall. Venus drying herself after her bath, a vase of perfumed ointments at her feet.
tracks.listen: How a statue made to fill a gap left by Napoleon's France became a masterpiece in its own right, and then lost its place.

tracks.title: Titian — The Concert
tracks.where: In the Sala di Venere, in front of Titian's Concert: three half-length men around a keyboard instrument.
tracks.what: Titian, The Concert, 1510–11, oil on canvas. A man in a dark fur-trimmed cloak plays a spinet, a Dominican monk with a viola da gamba touches his shoulder, and a young singer in a feathered cap stands on the left.
tracks.listen: A painting that passed for Giorgione for centuries, and a silent exchange of glances that leaves us outside.

tracks.title: Titian — Portrait of Pietro Aretino
tracks.where: In the Sala di Venere, in front of Titian's half-length portrait of a heavy bearded man in a wide red cloak and a gold chain.
tracks.what: Titian, Portrait of Pietro Aretino, early 1545, oil on canvas. Commissioned by Aretino and given by him to Duke Cosimo I de' Medici in October 1545.
tracks.listen: The most feared writer in Italy, the friend who painted him, and a complaint about the bill that tells us how Titian worked.

tracks.title: Titian — Portrait of a Lady (La Bella)
tracks.where: In the Sala di Venere, in front of Titian's half-length portrait of a young woman in a blue dress with burgundy sleeves. After this, the way out is through the Sala delle Nicchie.
tracks.what: Titian, Portrait of a Lady, known as La Bella, 1536–38, oil on canvas, 89 × 75.5 cm. Acquired by Francesco Maria della Rovere, Duke of Urbino; in Florence since 1631 with Vittoria della Rovere's collection.
tracks.listen: A woman nobody can name, the dress everyone can describe, the link back to the Magdalene, and the way out of the gallery.

tracks.title: Gallery of Modern Art — A different century
tracks.where: At the entrance to the Gallery of Modern Art on the second floor. From the stairs or lifts, follow the corridor and turn left; the rooms are numbered from 1 to 30 and run in a loop.
tracks.what: Thirty rooms of Italian painting and sculpture from the late 18th to the early 20th century, in rooms once used by the Lorraine grand dukes, with one of the richest Macchiaioli collections anywhere. The gallery opened in 1924.
tracks.listen: What "modern" meant when the gallery opened, and how the loop of rooms tells its story.

tracks.title: The Neoclassical rooms — marble, and Napoleon's years
tracks.where: In Rooms 1 and 2, the first rooms of the loop. Room 1 holds Tenerani's marble Psyche; Room 2 holds Benvenuti's large canvas of the Saxons' oath and Canova's colossal head of Napoleon.
tracks.what: Neoclassical sculpture and painting from the Napoleonic and early Lorraine years: Pietro Tenerani, Psyche Abandoned, c.1819; Pietro Benvenuti, The Saxons' Oath to Napoleon after the Battle of Jena, 1812; Giuseppe Bezzuoli, Portrait of Elisa Bonaparte Baciocchi, c.1814.
tracks.listen: What Neoclassicism wanted from art, and how Napoleon's family came to fill these first rooms.

tracks.title: Canova and workshop — Colossal Head of Napoleon
tracks.where: In Room 2 of the Gallery of Modern Art, in front of the colossal marble head of Napoleon.
tracks.what: Antonio Canova and his workshop, Colossal Head of Napoleon, marble, about 1810, after the portrait Canova modelled from life in Paris in 1802. Given to Grand Duke Leopold II by Louis Bonaparte in 1845.
tracks.listen: Five sittings with the First Consul, a face that became a bestseller, and the strange thank-you present that brought it to Florence.

tracks.title: Stefano Ussi — The Expulsion of the Duke of Athens
tracks.where: In Room 3 of the Gallery of Modern Art, in front of the huge history painting that fills one wall. Step back to take in the whole crowd.
tracks.what: Stefano Ussi, The Expulsion of the Duke of Athens, 1860, oil on canvas, 316 × 447 cm. First prize at the 1861 National Exhibition in Florence; gold medal at the 1867 Paris Exhibition.
tracks.listen: A tyrant thrown out of medieval Florence, painted at the very moment Tuscany was getting rid of its own ruler, with the painter hidden in the crowd.

tracks.title: Romanticism and history painting
tracks.where: In Room 5 of the Gallery of Modern Art, among the large history paintings. Rooms 6 to 9 follow.
tracks.what: Large-format history painting between Romanticism and Realism, including Giuseppe Bezzuoli's Entry of Charles VIII into Florence, 1829, and Giovanni Dupré's Dying Abel, 1846–51. Next: the first Macchiaioli experiments in Room 6, portraits in Rooms 7 and 8, landscapes in Room 9.
tracks.listen: How Italian painters used the past to talk about their present, and the turn toward painting what is in front of you.

tracks.title: The Macchiaioli rooms
tracks.where: In Rooms 10 to 13, the heart of the Macchiaioli display; Room 6 holds their first experiments. Play this as you enter Room 10.
tracks.what: The Tuscan Macchiaioli: the Banti collection and Boldini's Alaide Banti, 1866, in Room 10; Zandomeneghi's two portraits of Diego Martelli and two Pissarro landscapes in Room 11; Silvestro Lega's Singing a Stornello, 1867, in Room 12; Fattori's Italian Camp after the Battle of Magenta, 1862, in Room 13.
tracks.listen: Who the Macchiaioli were, the friends and patrons around them, and what to look for in each of these four rooms.

tracks.title: Giovanni Fattori — La Rotonda di Palmieri
tracks.where: In front of Fattori's Rotonda di Palmieri, if it is on view; the museum does not publish its room. It is tiny, only 12 by 35 centimetres, so look closely along the walls of the Macchiaioli rooms.
tracks.what: Giovanni Fattori, La Rotonda di Palmieri, 1866, oil on panel, 12 × 35 cm: seven women sitting in the shade of a long ochre awning at the Palmieri baths in Livorno.
tracks.listen: Why a picture the size of a long envelope is one of the best-loved in the gallery, and how much Fattori could say with a few patches of colour.

tracks.title: Toward the twentieth century
tracks.where: In Room 17, at the start of the last stretch of the loop, which runs on to Room 30.
tracks.what: Later nineteenth-century portraits and sculpture, Fattori's La cugina Argia (around 1861) in Room 19, Symbolism and Divisionism, and early twentieth-century Italian painting, some of it given by private collectors.
tracks.listen: How Italian painting split after the Macchiaioli, and how the loop ends.

tracks.title: The Palazzina della Meridiana
tracks.where: At the entrance to the Museum of Fashion and Costume, in the Palazzina della Meridiana on the second floor, reached from the landing along the corridor to the right and a staircase of two short flights, with a stair-lift. This is a dead end: you leave the way you came.
tracks.what: A small palace joined to the south wing of Palazzo Pitti, begun in 1776 by Gaspare Maria Paoletti for Grand Duke Pietro Leopoldo and completed in 1830 by Pasquale Poccianti. Since 1983 it has housed Italy's first state museum of fashion history, shown in rotation.
tracks.listen: How a beam of noon sunlight gave this building its name, and how the museum works.

tracks.title: The funeral clothes of Cosimo I, Eleonora di Toledo and Don Garzia
tracks.where: In front of the case with the three Medici funeral garments, which are permanently on display. The museum does not use room numbers.
tracks.what: The sixteenth-century burial clothes of Cosimo I de' Medici, his wife Eleonora di Toledo and their son Don Garzia, recovered from their tombs in San Lorenzo and shown after long and complex restoration.
tracks.listen: Three Medici, one terrible winter, and why Eleonora's dress is not the one in her famous portrait, whatever the legend says.

tracks.title: Three centuries of dress — the rotating display
tracks.where: Anywhere in the museum's galleries beyond the Medici garments. The displays rotate, so play this wherever you like; when you've finished, go back the way you came to the second-floor landing, then down one floor for the Royal Apartments, or down to the courtyard.
tracks.what: Clothes, accessories, jewellery and stage costumes from the eighteenth century to today, shown in rotation for conservation; the selection on view changes from time to time.
tracks.listen: How to read whatever is on display today, and how Italian fashion was launched on the world inside this very palace.

tracks.title: Imperial and Royal Apartments — Before your visit
tracks.where: At the Royal Apartments meeting point in the entrance atrium of the Palatine Gallery, first floor. Play this while you wait for your group; museum staff lead the visit itself, so please keep the audio paused inside. Reservation is compulsory; be at the meeting point about five minutes before your slot.
tracks.what: Fourteen state rooms in the south wing of the first floor, lived in by the Medici, the Habsburg-Lorraine and the House of Savoy, shown in a staff-led group visit of about 30 minutes that starts in the Green Room.
tracks.listen: Who lived in these rooms, and the handful of things worth watching for while the staff lead you through.

tracks.title: Imperial and Royal Apartments — After your visit
tracks.where: Anywhere once your staff-led group has left the Royal Apartments, on the first floor. From here the main stairs and lifts go down to the courtyard and the ground-floor museums.
tracks.what: A look back at the apartments you have just walked through: French imperial silk, a Medici alcove turned chapel, a Savoy throne room and the rooms of Queen Margherita.
tracks.listen: The answer to the parrot riddle, and how three dynasties layered their lives into one set of rooms.

tracks.title: Museum of Russian Icons — Cosimo III's summer apartment
tracks.where: Ground floor, off the Ammannati Courtyard: follow the signs for the Palatine Chapel and Russian Icons, and play this in the first frescoed room.
tracks.what: Four seventeenth-century frescoed rooms, restored and opened as the Museum of Russian Icons in 2022, hung with 78 Russian icons in gold and deep colour; captions in Italian, English and Russian.
tracks.listen: How a Medici summer apartment came to hold the oldest collection of Russian icons outside Russia, and what the gold is for.

tracks.title: The two oldest icons — The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist and "All Creatures Rejoice in You"
tracks.where: Room 1, in front of the small Beheading of Saint John the Baptist; its companion, the Mother of God "All Creatures Rejoice in You", should be nearby; its room is not stated officially.
tracks.what: Two Muscovite icons in tempera on panel with gilded-silver, filigree and enamel covers, each about 31 × 26 cm: "All Creatures Rejoice in You", c.1575–1600, and The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist, c.1590–1610. Both recorded in the palace's Chapel of Relics in 1639.
tracks.listen: Two small panels that were in the palace nearly four centuries before this museum existed, and how to read them.

tracks.title: The Palatine Chapel
tracks.where: The large central hall of the ground-floor apartment, beside the icon rooms. Stand near the middle, then look up at the vault and along the walls.
tracks.what: The court chapel created in 1766 for Pietro Leopoldo in the central hall of the 1661 summer apartment; painted by Luigi Ademollo in 1791–93, with the left choir loft completed in 1822–23. Altar in Florentine commesso incorporating parts made for the Chapel of the Princes at San Lorenzo; the Chigi Crucifix by Lorenz Rues and Antonio Raggi.
tracks.listen: How a reception hall became a court chapel, the painted New Testament scenes, and an altar made from the Medici's unfinished masterpiece.

tracks.title: The Ammannati Courtyard and the first view
tracks.where: At the back of the Ammannati Courtyard, with the palace behind you and the garden rising ahead; the Artichoke Fountain is on the terrace above. The Bacchino is reached from the left, east, side of the courtyard; an accessible tunnel under the loggia leads to the same little square.
tracks.what: The threshold of the Boboli Gardens: more than 30 hectares climbing the hill behind the palace, begun in 1549 for Eleonora di Toledo and reshaped over three centuries; now in the long Boboli 2030 restoration, with some areas fenced off but visible.
tracks.listen: Who began the garden, the single line it is built around, and an honest word about the restoration works.

tracks.title: The Bacchino — Morgante on a Tortoise
tracks.where: In the small square at the Bacchus exit, on the east side of the garden by the palace and the Vasari Corridor wall; the figure on the turtle sits in the fountain.
tracks.what: Morgante on a Tortoise, known as the Bacchino: a modern plaster copy of Valerio Cioli's marble of 1564–68, a fountain on this spot since 1579. The original marble is kept indoors.
tracks.listen: The real man behind the fountain, and the joke hidden in his turtle and his raised arm.

tracks.title: Buontalenti — the Grotta Grande
tracks.where: Beside the Bacchino, along the same east wall near the entrance to the Vasari Corridor. Stand in front of the façade; go inside only if the gate is open.
tracks.what: The Grotta Grande, or Buontalenti Grotto: begun in the 1550s as an aqueduct reservoir, given a façade by Vasari, and transformed by Bernardo Buontalenti from 1583. Bandinelli's Apollo and Ceres in the niches; inside, replicas of Michelangelo's four Prisoners, Vincenzo de' Rossi's Theseus and Helen, and Giambologna's Venus of about 1593.
tracks.listen: How a water tank became the strangest building in the garden, and the question it was built to ask.

tracks.title: The Grotta di Madama
tracks.where: Above and behind the Grotta Grande, in the small Giardino di Madama by the old convent wall, reached by the narrow side paths. The grotto is normally closed, so you see it from outside.
tracks.what: The Grotta di Madama, the oldest grotto in Boboli, built 1553–55 under Davide Fortini, Tribolo's son-in-law: an artificial-rock front in a stone frame with a white-marble doorway; inside, animal sculptures among stalactites and a vault painted with grotesques.
tracks.listen: The garden's first grotto, why Renaissance gardens wanted artificial caves, and who "Madama" was.

tracks.title: The Amphitheatre
tracks.where: At the edge of the amphitheatre, ideally at its palace end with the palace behind you and the obelisk in front. The stone tiers are fenced off for restoration; view it from the paths around the rim.
tracks.what: The amphitheatre: a stone quarry turned into a green theatre by Tribolo from about 1550 and rebuilt in stone by Giulio Parigi, finished in 1634. At its centre, an ancient Egyptian obelisk of Ramesses II, raised here in 1790, and a great red granite basin.
tracks.listen: How the palace's quarry became the Medici's open-air theatre, and the long journey of the obelisk.

tracks.title: Stoldo Lorenzi — the Neptune Fountain
tracks.where: On the terrace above the amphitheatre, on the path around the Neptune basin. The basin area is fenced off during restoration; view the fountain from the path.
tracks.what: The Neptune Fountain, known as the Forcone: a bronze Neptune with his trident by Stoldo Lorenzi, 1565–68, rising from a large basin set into the hillside.
tracks.listen: Why a sea god stands on a Tuscan hill, and how Florentines nicknamed him.

tracks.title: The Kaffeehaus and the view
tracks.where: At the Kaffeehaus, the small pavilion with a domed, turreted roof on the eastern side of the upper garden. Stand at the terrace edge, facing the city.
tracks.what: The Kaffeehaus by Zanobi del Rosso, 1774–85, for Grand Duke Pietro Leopoldo; restored in 2022 as part of Boboli 2030. Nearby, the Garden of Ganymede, with a sixteenth-century marble Ganymede on the eagle attributed to Giovanni Battista Lorenzi.
tracks.listen: The best view of Florence from the garden, and a grand duke's pavilion for drinks on a walk.

tracks.title: Giambologna and Pietro Tacca — Abundance
tracks.where: At the foot of the colossal statue of Abundance, at the top of the central axis, just below the Knight's Garden. If the statue is fenced off for restoration, view it from the nearest path. Turn around to look back down the hill toward the palace.
tracks.what: Abundance, a colossal marble begun by Giambologna and completed after his death by his pupil Pietro Tacca, set up here in 1637. She holds a sheaf of wheat and a horn of plenty.
tracks.listen: How a portrait of a grand duchess may have become an allegory, and why she stands exactly here.

tracks.title: The Viottolone
tracks.where: On the Viottolone, the long cypress avenue running down the south-western slope from the top of the hill to the Isolotto. Part of the labyrinth of paths beside it is fenced off for restoration; the avenue itself is open.
tracks.what: A long, straight avenue between tall cypresses, with statues at intervals, laid out around 1612 as the garden was pushed south under Cosimo II and Ferdinando II. Fifty-three new cypresses were planted in recent years.
tracks.listen: How the garden grew south, and why a four-hundred-year-old avenue has young trees.

tracks.title: Giambologna — the Isolotto and Oceanus
tracks.where: At the rim of the oval Isolotto basin, at the foot of the Viottolone. The island's inner area is closed for restoration, so view the fountain from the outer ring. The Porta Romana gate is right beside the pool.
tracks.what: The Isolotto, a large oval basin of 1618 with a central island holding a copy of Giambologna's marble Oceanus, finished by 1576, with the Nile, Ganges and Euphrates below; the original is in the Bargello. Around the pool, Perseus on horseback, and groups of peasants at their games.
tracks.listen: A giant who isn't the original, the whole world in one fountain, and the ordinary people around the rim.

tracks.title: The Limonaia
tracks.where: Outside the Limonaia, the long, low Lemon House on the western, Via Romana side of the garden, north of the Isolotto toward the palace. Its gates are closed for restoration; view it from outside. The Annalena gate is close by.
tracks.what: The Lemon House, built 1777–78 by Zanobi del Rosso for Pietro Leopoldo on the site of Cosimo III's menagerie, enlarged by Giuseppe Cacialli in 1816. About 106 metres long and facing south, it shelters some 500 potted citrus trees through the winter.
tracks.listen: From a grand-ducal zoo to a winter home for lemons, and the Medici passion for strange citrus.

tracks.title: Ways out of the garden
tracks.where: Play it on the way to whichever gate you choose: Palazzo Pitti through the Ammannati Courtyard, Annalena on Via Romana, Porta Romana beside the Isolotto, or Forte di Belvedere at the top of the hill.
tracks.what: The four official entrances and exits of the Boboli Gardens, and where each one leaves you.
tracks.listen: Where each of the four gates comes out, the story behind the Annalena name, and an idea for a return visit.

tracks.title: Closing
tracks.where: Anywhere you like once you've finished, at whichever gate or door you came out of: a bench, a café table, the street outside.
tracks.what: The closing reflection on Palazzo Pitti and the Boboli Gardens.
tracks.listen: What the palace and garden add up to, who they belong to now, and where to go next.
